lessons.title: Five on five, one hoop
lessons.objective: Explain how a game is won and what each basket is worth.

payload.prompt: How does a basketball game end?

options.text: When the clock reaches zero, the team with the most points wins.
When one team scores 100 points.
When one team gets 10 baskets ahead.

explanation.correct: Exactly right. Basketball is won by points, not by reaching a score target. The game ends when time runs out, and the higher score wins.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Basketball games have fixed lengths (quarters or halves), and either team can win by any margin. It is not about hitting a magic number.
explanation.sayThisLine: Time runs out, higher score wins.

payload.prompt: What is a three-pointer worth?

options.text: Three points.
Two points plus a bonus point.
Two points, same as any field goal.

explanation.correct: Right. A shot from behind the arc is worth 3 points. Free throws are 1, regular field goals are 2, and threes are 3.
explanation.incorrect: Not that one. Three-pointers are their own scoring tier: free throws (1), field goals (2), three-pointers (3).
explanation.sayThisLine: Free throw one, field goal two, three-pointer three.

payload.prompt: A player is fouled while shooting a three-pointer and misses. How many free throws?

options.text: Two free throws.
Three free throws, because it was a three.
One free throw, the standard.

explanation.correct: Correct. A non-shooting foul on a shooter (called a shooting foul) gives two free throws if the shot misses, or one free throw (plus the made basket) if it goes in. The arc distance does not change that.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Shooting fouls always give two free throws on a miss, regardless of how far away the shooter was. If the shot goes in, it is one more (the and-one).
explanation.sayThisLine: Shooting foul on a miss: two shots.

payload.prompt: Complete the scoring breakdown.
payload.template: A free throw is worth {{one-point}}, a field goal inside the arc is worth {{two-point}}, and a three-pointer is worth {{three-point}}.

explanation.correct: Perfect. You have got the scoring tier system down. These three categories cover every possible basket.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The scoring values are fixed: free throw (1), field goal (2), three-pointer (3). The farthest basket is worth the most.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: Whether the final score was higher.
Whether they scored all threes.
Whether everyone played the whole game.
Whether they made 50 points.

payload.translation: She is asking if your team finished with a higher score than the other team.

followUps.why: You are giving the final score, which answers the question directly.

followUps.line: Who were you watching?
followUps.why: This is a natural follow-up that keeps the conversation going.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Remember: you don't need to know the stats to follow a game. Just keep it real.

lessons.title: The court, line by line
lessons.objective: Name the lines and zones you will hear about every game.

payload.prompt: Tap the half-court line.

diagram.alt: A regulation basketball court with centerline, sidelines, baselines, and other markings.

explanation.correct: Yes! The half-court line divides the court into two halves. It is the dividing line from sideline to sideline at the center.
explanation.incorrect: Not that one. The half-court line runs across the middle of the court, dividing it into two equal halves.
explanation.sayThisLine: The half-court line is in the middle.

payload.prompt: Tap the three-point arc.

diagram.alt: A basketball court with the three-point line highlighted as an arc beyond the painted lane.

explanation.correct: Exactly! The three-point line is the arc that circles the court at a distance (23 ft 9 in at the top in the NBA). Shots from beyond this line count 3.
explanation.incorrect: Not that area. The three-point line is the arc on the perimeter; shots from beyond it are worth 3 points.
explanation.sayThisLine: Beyond the arc is three points.

payload.prompt: Tap the paint (the key).

diagram.alt: A basketball court with the painted lane highlighted under the basket.

explanation.correct: Right! The paint is the rectangular area under the basket from the baseline to the free-throw line. It is called the paint because of its bright color.
explanation.incorrect: Not that spot. The paint is the painted lane directly under the basket, the most congested area where big men operate.
explanation.sayThisLine: The paint is where the action happens inside.

payload.prompt: Match each line to what it marks.

pairs.definition: The line 15 feet from the backboard where players shoot free throws.
The line at each end of the court marking the end of play.
A 4-foot arc under the basket where defenders cannot draw charges.

distractorDefinitions: The line that divides the court in half.
The arc 23 feet 9 inches from the basket in the NBA.

explanation.summary: You have the court's most important lines down. These mark where special rules apply.

payload.prompt: How far is the NBA three-point line at the top of the key?

options.text: 23 feet 9 inches.
22 feet.
25 feet.

explanation.correct: Yes. The NBA three-point line is 23 ft 9 in at the top and 22 ft in the corners. The corner is closer, so corner threes are highly efficient.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The NBA three-point line is 23 ft 9 in at the top of the arc, though it is 22 ft in the corners.
explanation.sayThisLine: 23 9 at the top, 22 in the corners.

payload.prompt: Why is the area under the basket called the paint?

options.text: Because the lane is painted a bright color on the court.
Because only painted players can shoot there.
Because it was invented by the painter of the court.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The paint is the rectangular area under the basket that is painted in a bright, contrasting color. Hence the name.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The name simply comes from the paint color used to mark the lane on the court floor.

lessons.title: Two clocks: game and shot
lessons.objective: Explain the game clock, shot clock and why 24 seconds matters.

payload.prompt: How long is an NBA game (regulation)?

explanation.correct: Right! An NBA game is 48 minutes in four 12-minute quarters. That does not include halftime or timeouts, which stretch the real time.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. An NBA game is 48 minutes in four 12-minute quarters. College and the WNBA differ.

payload.prompt: What is the NBA shot clock limit?

explanation.correct: Exactly right. The shot clock is 24 seconds in the NBA and WNBA. A team must get a shot off within that time or lose the ball.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The NBA shot clock is 24 seconds. College is 30 seconds.

payload.prompt: How do college men play their game?

options.text: Two 20-minute halves.
Four 12-minute quarters like the NBA.
Four 10-minute quarters like the WNBA.

explanation.correct: Right. College men play in halves (two 20-minute periods), which gives a different rhythm than the NBA's quarters. Women's college is moving to quarters.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. College men still use halves, not quarters. The rhythm is different from the NBA and WNBA.

payload.prompt: If a game is tied at the end of regulation, what happens?

options.text: An extra period (overtime) is played until a winner emerges.
The game ends in a tie.
The teams replay the entire game.

explanation.correct: Yes. Overtime is a five-minute extra period in the NBA and WNBA. If it is still tied, more overtimes are played.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Basketball always ends with a winner. Overtime is played until one team scores more.

payload.prompt: Explain the shot clock rule.
payload.template: A team has {{time-limit}} seconds to get a shot off before losing the ball. In the NBA, the clock resets to {{reset-time}} after an offensive rebound.

explanation.correct: Perfect. The NBA shot clock forces action: 24 seconds for a fresh possession, 14 after an offensive rebound. This keeps the game pace fast.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The NBA shot clock is 24 seconds on a new possession, 14 after an offensive rebound. College is 30 with no reduction.

lessons.title: Who has the ball?
lessons.objective: Follow possession: jump ball, inbounds, turnovers and the alternating arrow.

payload.prompt: Which is a turnover?

options.text: A pass that goes out of bounds.
A made basket.
A shot that bounces off the rim.

explanation.correct: Right. A turnover is any loss of possession that is not a shot or a foul. Out of bounds, traveling, and steals are all turnovers.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A turnover is a loss of possession. Mistakes like traveling or passing out of bounds cause turnovers.

payload.prompt: What is an inbound pass?

options.text: A pass from out of bounds to start or restart play.
A pass thrown from inside the court to the perimeter.
A catch made after the ball bounces in from the sideline.

explanation.correct: Exactly. An inbound is the pass that brings the ball from out of bounds into play. The inbounder has five seconds to do it.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. An inbound is the first pass from out of bounds. It starts a new possession.

payload.prompt: At the start of the game, who jumps?

scene.alt: A basketball game starting with two centers at center court.

explanation.correct: Right. At the very start of the game, the referee throws the ball up and the two nearest players (usually centers) jump to tap it. After that, the alternating arrow is used.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The game starts with a jump ball, where two players jump to tap the ball. The arrow takes over after the first possession.

payload.prompt: A player shoots and misses. The other team tips the rebound away. Is it still a possession change?

scene.alt: A rebound scenario where one team shoots and another team gets the rebound.

choices.label: Yes, possession changed the moment the rebound was tipped.
No, possession does not change on a rebound.

explanation.correct: Correct. A rebound is a possession change. The team that secures the ball after a missed shot now has possession.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Any change in which team has the ball is a possession change. A rebound (getting the ball after a missed shot) counts.

payload.prompt: Order the events at the start of a game.

items.text: Jump ball at center court; the two centers tap.
From then on, the alternating arrow decides jump-ball situations.
One team gets the first possession from the jump ball.

explanation.correct: Perfect. You have the game's opening sequence right. The first possession goes to whoever wins the initial jump ball.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The game starts with a jump ball, then the arrow is used for all other jump-ball situations.

lessons.title: How one possession flows
lessons.objective: Order the phases of a possession from bring-up to shot or foul.

payload.prompt: Order the phases of a typical offensive possession.

items.text: Bring-up: the guard gets the ball up court quickly.
items.why: This is the first phase of every possession.

items.text: Set up: the offense gets into their formation and starts moving the ball.
items.why: After clearing half-court, the team arranges their setup.

items.text: Finish: the ball handler shoots, passes for a score, or turns it over.
items.why: Every possession ends with a shot, turnover, or foul.

explanation.correct: Exactly right. Bring-up, then setup and ball movement, then a finish (shot, turnover, or foul). This is the rhythm of every possession.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Possessions flow from bringing the ball up court, through the offensive setup, to a finish (shot or turnover).

payload.prompt: What happens after a missed shot?

items.text: A player from either team grabs the rebound.
items.why: Rebounding is the first step after a miss.

items.text: The other team quickly breaks the other way.
items.why: Transition is the scramble when possession changes.

items.text: The defense gets back or the offense scores quick.
items.why: This determines if it is a transition bucket or settled defense.

explanation.correct: Right. After a rebound, transition begins—the scramble to either score quick or get the defense set.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. After a miss, someone rebounds, and then transition (the fast break) happens.

payload.prompt: What is half-court offense?

options.text: The offensive set run from a formation at the top of the key after the team is set.
An offense that only scores from the halfway line.
Any offense played in the first half of the game.

explanation.correct: Right. Half-court offense is the deliberate set after the team gets into formation, not the transition fast break.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Half-court offense is the set play run when the team is not in transition, usually from the top of the key.

payload.prompt: Why is transition defense hard?

options.text: Fewer defenders are back to stop the offense before they set up.
The rules change during transition.
The offense is allowed to travel during transition.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Transition is a race: the offense is ahead, and the defense scrambles to get back. Easy buckets happen here.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Transition is tough for defense because the offense is ahead in numbers and racing to score before the defense is set.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They just scored on the break.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: They scored quickly on a transition fast break.
They broke a game record.
Someone broke a bone and they scored anyway.
They scored from the broken play (no set).

payload.translation: The other team got an easy, quick basket because your team's defense was not set when they got the ball.

followUps.line: Yeah, nobody was ready.
followUps.why: You are validating her observation that the defense got caught out of position.

followUps.line: Do they always run that fast?
followUps.why: This is a genuine follow-up that shows you are paying attention to their style.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The break is just a fast transition. Keep it simple.

lessons.title: The five positions
lessons.objective: Match guard, forward and center to what they usually do.

payload.prompt: Match each position to their main job.

pairs.definition: Sets up the offense, controls the pace and initiates ball movement.
Scores from outside, hits three-pointers and is often taller than the point guard.
The tallest player, plays near the basket on offense and defense, rebounds.

distractorDefinitions: Guards the other team's best player.
Shoots more often than any other position.

explanation.summary: You have the traditional position roles down. Each has a main job, though modern basketball is blurring these lines.

payload.prompt: What do the forwards do?

pairs.definition: A versatile forward who scores inside and out, defends multiple positions.
A big man who plays closer to the basket, rebounds and finishes close to the rim.

distractorDefinitions: The forward who is smallest in height.
The forward who has the most power.

explanation.summary: The two forward positions have different jobs: the small forward is versatile, the power forward is a paint player.

payload.prompt: Tap where the point guard usually starts.

diagram.alt: A basketball court showing the typical starting positions of the five players.

explanation.correct: Right. The point guard starts at the top of the key (around the center, back), since they run the offense.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The point guard runs the offense, so they start at the top of the key, at the back.

payload.prompt: Why is the point guard often the smallest player?

options.text: Speed and ball-handling skills matter more than size for running offense.
Height is not allowed for the point guard position.
Smaller players score more points.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Point guards need to be fast, nimble and skilled with the ball. Height is less important than control and vision.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Point guards are often smaller because speed and ball-handling are what matter most for running the offense.

payload.prompt: A player is 6'11". What position are they likely to play?

options.text: Center or power forward (a 'big').
Shooting guard.
Point guard.

explanation.correct: Right. At 6'11", a player is in the 'big' category and usually plays near the basket as a center or power forward.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A player that tall plays in the paint or near the basket, not on the perimeter.

lessons.title: Roles over labels: positionless
lessons.objective: Decode wing, big, 3-and-D and why fans say positionless.

payload.prompt: Match each label to what it means.

pairs.definition: A guard or forward who plays on the perimeter; expected to shoot and defend multiple opponents.
A center or power forward; a taller player who plays near the basket.
A player strong at two things: making three-pointers and defending. A solid role player, not a star.

distractorDefinitions: A player who makes three baskets and has no defensive weakness.
A position that does not exist in traditional basketball.

explanation.summary: These are modern labels that describe what a player does, not just their position. They reflect how the game has evolved.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: Players are defined by what they do, not by a rigid position label.
The team has players with no job on the court.
All five players rotate to every position equally.
The team is not using a coach or strategy.

payload.translation: The team is flexible. Their players can guard any opponent and play any spot, based on skill rather than position number.

followUps.line: That is how the Warriors play, right?
followUps.why: You are connecting her comment to a real example, showing you are learning.

followUps.line: Does that help their defense?
followUps.why: A genuine question about whether it works.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Positionless just means flexible. You do not need to name every role.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Their big can shoot threes. That stretches the floor.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: A tall player who shoots threes pulls defenders away from the rim.
The big player makes very long passes.
The big player is unusually tall and skinny.
The court looks wider when the big shoots.

payload.translation: A big man (center or power forward) who can shoot from distance pulls defenders away from the paint, opening lanes.

followUps.line: So it opens up the inside for cutters?
followUps.why: You are thinking about the effect—good follow-up.

followUps.line: Is he a good shooter from distance?
followUps.why: A real question about his game.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Just understand: shooters pull defenders out. It is not complicated.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: He is a solid role player off the bench.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: A bench player with a specific, well-defined job; a key contributor.
A player who only plays one position.
A player acting in a movie or TV show.
A player who is not very good.

payload.translation: He comes off the bench and does his job well—maybe shooting threes, rebounding, or defending. Reliable, not a star.

followUps.line: What does he do best for the team?
followUps.why: This is a great follow-up; you are showing interest in his role.

followUps.line: Has he been here long?
followUps.why: A natural question about whether he is new.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Role players are crucial. Do not dismiss them as 'just bench players.'

payload.prompt: What does positionless basketball mean?

options.text: Players are defined by what they do, not a rigid position. Anyone can guard anyone and play anywhere.
The team does not have a center or point guard.
The team has no strategy or structure.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Positionless basketball prioritizes skills (defense, shooting, ball-handling) over position number. It is flexible and modern.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Positionless means roles are fluid and based on skills, not rigid labels.

lessons.title: Reading a box score
lessons.objective: Read a box score line and say what happened out loud.

payload.prompt: Fill in the stat abbreviations.

explanation.correct: Perfect. These are the standard abbreviations on a box score: PTS (points), REB (rebounds), AST (assists), STL (steals).
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The standard box score abbreviations are PTS, REB, AST, STL, BLK, TO (turnovers), and FG% (field-goal percentage).

payload.prompt: Complete the definition.
payload.template: A {{double}} is double digits in two categories (like points and rebounds). A {{triple}} is double digits in three categories (like points, rebounds, and assists).

explanation.correct: Right. A double-double is 10+ in two stats; a triple-double is 10+ in three. These are highlights, rare achievements.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A double-double is double digits (10+) in two categories; a triple-double is triple digits in three.

payload.prompt: A player shoots 15 times and makes 10. What is their FG%?

explanation.correct: Right. 10 makes out of 15 attempts is 10/15 = 0.667 = 67%. A high FG% is a sign of efficiency.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. 10 out of 15 is roughly 67%, or about two-thirds. That is a high, efficient percentage.

payload.prompt: What does a +15 plus-minus mean?

options.text: Your team outscored the opponent by 15 while this player was on the court.
The player scored 15 more points than last game.
The player has 15 more assists than turnovers.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Plus-minus is the team margin while a player plays. +15 means the team was ahead by 15 in their minutes.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Plus-minus tracks the team margin while the player is on the court, not individual stats.

payload.prompt: What does a box score show?

options.text: Each player's stats (points, rebounds, assists, etc.) for a game.
Only the box shapes drawn on the court.
The scores of all games in a season.

explanation.correct: Right. A box score is a table of every player's stats for that game: points, rebounds, assists, field-goal percentage and more.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A box score is a stats table for each player in a game, showing their production.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Look at her line: 22 points, 8 boards, 11 dimes, 2 steals.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: A player's stats from the game: points, rebounds, assists, steals.
A player's jersey number and position.
The player's scoring in four different quarters.
A recipe or instructions the player follows.

payload.translation: She is reading the box score of a player's game: 22 points, 8 rebounds (boards), 11 assists (dimes), 2 steals.

followUps.line: That is a triple-double!
followUps.why: You are recognizing the achievement—10+ in three stats.

followUps.line: Was she the leading scorer?
followUps.why: A real follow-up question about where 22 ranks on the team.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Box score 'slang' is just casual shorthand. Do not pretend you know every abbreviation.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: He was plus-22, but his team still lost.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: He played great (team was up 22 while he was on court), but the team lost overall.
He scored 22 points more than his opponent.
He has 22 wins and 0 losses.
He is 22 years old and winning.

payload.translation: His individual performance was excellent (team outscored the opponent by 22 while he was playing), but the team lost the game because others played poorly.

followUps.line: So the bench let them down?
followUps.why: You are connecting the idea that his minutes were good but other players struggled.

followUps.line: Did he play the whole game?
followUps.why: A real question about how many minutes he played.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Plus-minus can be misleading (it depends on teammates), but it is a useful stat.

lessons.objective: Handle a casual basketball text without bluffing.

payload.title: Casual texting after a win
payload.setting: Texting your crush after their team wins a close game.

replies.text: Yeah, I saw it. That was close!
replies.theirResponse: Right? I was stressed the whole fourth quarter.
replies.coachNote: You watched and showed genuine interest. Perfect.

replies.text: I missed it. Tell me what happened!
replies.theirResponse: They almost lost but pulled it out at the end. It was crazy.
replies.coachNote: Asking her to tell you is honest and keeps her talking. Even better.

replies.text: Nah, basketball is not really my thing.
replies.theirResponse: Oh, okay. I thought you might be into it.

exchanges.theirMessage: Are you going to watch the next game?

replies.theirResponse: Fair. Let me know if you want to catch one together.

That kills the vibe. If she cares about it, it matters.

followUps.why: A question about whether this is a pattern.

The player took the shot at the wrong time of day.
